jurors.reason: As a lawyer I see a probable minor (a high school senior in Korea is usually under 19) planning to take payouts, run a business and publish games with no one in the record having checked parental consent, platform age limits, tax or game-rating rules, so it should not go ahead as described.
jurors.fact: Both sides leave open "whether a minor can legally receive payouts" (prosecution's missing-from-record list; defense rebuttal point 5 calls it "a real unknown"), and nothing in the case addresses it.
jurors.flip: The case stated the user's legal age and a verified payout route (for example a guardian-held account or an adult-eligible platform, with tax and any business-registration duties confirmed) before any money or published product is involved.

jurors.reason: I would never open a shop with no product, no customer and no idea how the first won comes in, and a senior with exams ahead is the only one to staff it on Monday morning while the 500,000 KRW sits there with nothing to bring it back.
jurors.fact: The record names no product, sales channel, price or basis for the 1,000,000 KRW target, and the defense itself conceded this in its opening and again in its rebuttal.
jurors.flip: The user named one specific product and one specific sales channel, with a small first spend and a fixed weekly hour limit that puts exam preparation first.

jurors.reason: As an investor I would not fund a plan that names no product, no buyer and no way to earn, where up to 500,000 KRW is at risk against a 1,000,000 KRW target with no stated basis and an unpriced cost in a senior's exam-year hours.
jurors.fact: The defense itself conceded that the record does not say which games or websites, or how they would earn (ads, sales, subscriptions), and that the 1,000,000 KRW target has no stated basis.
jurors.flip: The case named a specific product, a sales channel and a revenue estimate behind the 1,000,000 KRW target, with a spending stop-loss well below 500,000 KRW and a fixed weekly hour cap that puts exams first.

jurors.reason: The burden is on the proponent, and the record holds only a goal and a ceiling on spending, with no product, no revenue route and no basis for the 1,000,000 KRW target, so what is offered is hope, not proof.
jurors.fact: The defense itself conceded that the record does not say which games or websites, how they would earn, or what the 1,000,000 KRW target rests on.
jurors.flip: The case named a specific product, a sales channel and a revenue estimate with its basis, plus a weekly hour cap that puts exam preparation first and confirmation that a minor can legally receive payouts.

jurors.reason: As an engineer I can build almost anything the AI setup can write, but "games, websites, etc." is not a spec, and what breaks first is not the code but getting users and getting paid, which the plan does not address.
jurors.fact: The record names no product, channel or monetization method, and it is silent on whether a minor can receive payouts, so there is nothing concrete to build, ship or test against the 1,000,000 KRW target.
jurors.flip: The case named one small, specific product with a defined sales or ad channel and a working payout route for a minor, with a weekly hour cap that puts exam study first.

jurors.reason: "Make games and websites, etc." is not something anyone would talk about, share or come back to next week, because there's no actual thing and no reason for a single person to show up.
jurors.fact: The defense itself conceded the record names no game, no site, no way it earns, and no basis for the 1,000,000 KRW target, so there is nothing yet for anyone to care about.
jurors.flip: The case named one specific game or site aimed at a specific group of people (for example, other Korean students) with a place to reach them and a way they pay or click.
